Circumcenter On Angle Bisector

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: Drag the corners of a triangle and watch the circle through two corners and the middle point: its centre always lands on the line from the top corner.
How to play: Drag A, B or C with a mouse or finger, or focus a corner and use the arrow keys. Press the Show buttons to reveal more lines, then Check the claims.
Look for the math

Move a corner of the triangle. Three special points move with it, and the circle through B, I and C keeps its centre on the line from A to I. That is the whole droodle: a fact that stays true for every triangle.

Where I comes from

Each corner has an angle bisector, a line that cuts its angle into two equal parts. The three of them meet at one point, the incenter I. So AI is the bisector at A, and I is equally far from all three sides. The applet finds I by intersecting the bisectors from B and C; the logic test checks that this is the same point as the side-length formula for the incenter on hundreds of triangles, acute, right and obtuse.

The excenter on the same line

At B and C there are also outer bisectors: each one is at right angles to the inner bisector at that corner. They meet at E, the excenter opposite A. Because the outer and inner bisectors are perpendicular, the angles IBE and ICE are right angles. The applet marks K and L, the midpoints of IB and IC, with little right-angle corners; those confirm that O, the centre of the circle through B, I and C, sits on the perpendicular bisectors of the two chords.

A circle with diameter IE

Since both IBE and ICE are right angles, B and C lie on the circle whose diameter is IE: a right angle always subtends a diameter. That circle is exactly the one drawn here, the circumcircle of triangle BIC. Its centre O is the midpoint of IE. And because A, I and E lie on one straight line, O lies on AI too — which is the problem from Andreescu and Gelca's collection that the original page illustrates. The logic test verifies every link in this chain: IO = IB = IC, O is the midpoint of IE, and A, I, O, E are collinear.

One more surprise

The original page adds that O also lies on the circumcircle of ABC. This is not a side remark: it holds for every non-degenerate triangle tried, and the test compares it with an independent computation of that circle. Press Show hint to see E and the two outer bisectors, Show premise for K, L and the chord midpoints, and Show statement to pick out AI. Press Check the claims to test your current triangle.

Try making a very long, flat triangle: the centre O may leave the picture, but it still lies on the line AI and on the circle through A, B and C.
